content: 1. Acquisition refers to the process of capturing and storing image data during an imaging procedure. 2. The apex of the heart is the rounded tip of the heart, formed by the left ventricle. The myocardium in this region is thinner compared to other parts of the ventricle. 3. An artifact is a false structure or feature in an image or data that arises from the imaging technique or equipment rather than the actual object being imaged. 4. Axial refers to a plane or section created by cutting the body or a part of it at right angles to its long axis. If the body is upright, this plane is parallel to the horizon. 5. B or Bo is the standard symbol for the constant magnetic field generated by the main magnet in an MRI scanner. 6. B1 is the conventional symbol used to denote the radiofrequency (RF) magnetic field in MRI. 7. The base of the heart is the region formed by the atria and the roots of the great vessels, located opposite the apex and considered the top of the heart. 8. Cine imaging involves capturing a series of images in rapid succession over time and displaying them as a dynamic movie. This technique is often used to study motion, such as joint or spinal movements. 9. Contrast in imaging refers to the relative difference in signal intensities between adjacent regions of an image. It is influenced by imaging parameters like TE, TR, and TI, as well as tissue properties such as proton density and T1 or T2 relaxation times. 10. Coronal refers to a plane or section created by cutting the body from side to side, parallel to the coronal suture of the skull. 11. Echo planar imaging (EPI) is a technique that uses rapid gradient reversals to generate a series of gradient echo signals, reducing signal loss or dephasing. 12. An echo train is a sequence of 180° RF rephasing pulses and their corresponding echoes, used in fast spin echo (FSE) sequences. 13. Fast spin echo (FSE) is a pulse sequence characterized by rapid application of 180° rephasing pulses and multiple echoes, with phase encoding gradients changing for each echo. 14. Fat saturation (Fat-Sat) is a technique that selectively suppresses fat signals by saturating fat protons before data acquisition, requiring a homogeneous magnetic field and precise frequency calibration. 15. Fat suppression is a method, often using STIR sequences, to eliminate fat signals from images, improving diagnostic clarity. 16. 17. Field echo (FE), also called gradient echo, is an echo generated by reversing the magnetic field gradient to counteract position-dependent phase shifts. 18. Flip angle (FA) is the angle to which the net magnetization is rotated relative to the main magnetic field by an RF excitation pulse, influencing the characteristics of field echo sequences. 19. Fourier transform (FT) is a mathematical process used in MRI to separate and analyze the frequency components of signals, enabling spatial reconstruction of images from raw data. 20. Gadolinium (Gd) is a paramagnetic contrast agent used in MRI to enhance signal intensities by shortening T1 relaxation times in surrounding tissues. 21. Gating involves synchronizing image acquisition with physiological motion, such as cardiac or respiratory cycles, to reduce motion artifacts. 22. Image acquisition time is the duration required to collect all the data needed for an image, excluding the time for image reconstruction. 23. Image reconstruction is the mathematical process of converting raw data from the acquisition phase into a visual image. 24. Inversion recovery is an imaging sequence involving 180° and 90° pulses to produce a heavily T1-weighted signal, defined by parameters like inversion time (TI), repetition time (TR), and echo time (TE). 25. Inversion time (TI) is the interval between the 180° inversion pulse and the 90° excitation pulse in an inversion recovery sequence. 26. K-space is a data matrix containing raw image data before processing, with each line corresponding to a specific phase-encoding level. 27. The Larmor equation describes the relationship between the precession frequency of nuclear magnetic moments, the magnetic field strength (Bo), and the gyromagnetic ratio (γ). 28. Larmor frequency is the specific frequency at which magnetic resonance can be excited and detected, directly proportional to the magnetic field strength. 29. Magnetic resonance refers to the absorption or emission of energy by atomic nuclei in a magnetic field when exposed to RF pulses at the Larmor frequency. 30. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) is an imaging technique used to visualize blood vessels, such as the Circle of Willis or carotid arteries. 31. Maximum intensity projection (MIP) is a processing technique for MRA images that displays the highest intensity values along a projection ray through the imaging volume. 32. MR imaging uses magnetic resonance principles to create diagnostic images based on tissue properties like proton density, T1 and T2 relaxation times, and flow characteristics. 33. Noise refers to unwanted background interference that degrades image quality. 34. Oblique refers to a plane or section that is not perpendicular to the standard xyz coordinate system, such as long and short axis views of the heart. 35. Orthogonal refers to a plane or section that is perpendicular to the xyz coordinate system. 36. Phase contrast is an MRA technique that uses phase shifts in flowing protons to generate vascular images. 37. Phase encoding is the process of spatially locating MR signals by altering the phase of spins in one dimension using a magnetic field gradient, enabling precise image reconstruction. 38. A pixel is the smallest two-dimensional unit of a digital image display. 39. Planar imaging involves the slow precession of a spinning body's axis, such as the magnetic moment of a nucleus, under the influence of a torque. 40. A pulse sequence is a predefined set of RF and gradient pulses, repeated during a scan, that determines the characteristics of the MR signal and resulting images. 41. The receiver is the component of MRI equipment that detects and amplifies RF signals, including preamplifiers and demodulators. 42. A receiver coil is an antenna within the imaging volume that detects NMR signals, with various designs like solenoidal, planar, or phased array coils. 43. Reconstruction is the process of creating a visual image from raw k-space data using mathematical techniques like Fourier transformation. 44. Region of interest (ROI) refers to the specific anatomical area being imaged. 45. Relaxation time describes the time it takes for spins to return to equilibrium after excitation, with T1 representing longitudinal relaxation and T2 representing transverse relaxation. 46. Repetition time (TR) is the interval between successive pulse sequences applied to the same slice, influencing image contrast and scan time. 47. Resonance occurs when a system vibrates at a natural frequency due to a periodic stimulus, facilitating energy exchange. 48. Sagittal refers to a plane or section dividing the body into left and right parts, viewed from the cut surface. 49. Saturation recovery is a pulse sequence that generates proton density-dependent signals by allowing spins to return to equilibrium before the next pulse. 50. Selective excitation targets specific regions for excitation by controlling the RF pulse frequency and applying a magnetic field gradient. 51. Scan time is the total duration required to acquire all data for an image. 52. Signal averaging improves the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) by averaging multiple acquisitions under similar conditions. 53. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is the ratio of signal amplitude to background noise, affecting image quality and influenced by factors like coil type and imaging parameters. 54. A slice refers to the planar region or section of the body being imaged. 55. 56. 57. Spin-echo (SE) is the reappearance of an NMR signal after dephasing, achieved through specific RF pulse sequences or gradient pulses, and used to control T1 or T2 contrast. 58. Steady-state free precession refers to a gradient echo sequence where a steady state of transverse and longitudinal magnetization is maintained due to closely spaced RF pulses. 59. STIR (Short T1 Inversion Recovery) is a specialized inversion recovery sequence that suppresses fat signals by setting the inversion time to 0.69 times the T1 of fat. 60. A surface coil is a type of receiver coil placed directly over the region of interest to enhance signal sensitivity and improve SNR. 61. T1 is the longitudinal relaxation time, representing the time for spins to realign with the external magnetic field after excitation. 62. T1-weighted images are created using short TE and TR times, with contrast primarily determined by T1 signals. 63. T2 is the transverse relaxation time, representing the time for loss of phase coherence among spins due to spin-spin interactions. 64. T2 (T2-star) is the time constant for loss of phase coherence due to both magnetic field inhomogeneities and spin-spin relaxation, resulting in faster signal decay than T2. 65. T2-weighted images are created using longer TE and TR times, with contrast primarily determined by T2 signals. 66. TE (echo time) is the time between the application of the 90° pulse and the peak of the echo signal in spin echo and inversion recovery sequences. 67. Tesla (T) is the unit of magnetic flux density, with 1 Tesla equal to 10,000 gauss. 68. Time of flight (TOF) is an MRA technique that relies on the flow of unsaturated blood into a presaturated slice to create bright vascular images without contrast agents. 69. TR (repetition time) is the interval between successive pulse sequences applied to the same slice, influencing image contrast and scan time.
